Given the score rollback and comment freeze, we thought it might be helpful to provide a concise summary of the discussion to date. Our initial responses were written to address reviewers’ concerns individually and in detail, rather than for a single person making a holistic judgment. This comment therefore serves to summarize the paper, reviewers’ concerns, and our responses. 
___

## Summary of the Paper (post-rebuttal)

We empirically explore the failure modes of context length extrapolation in Transformers with RoPE, and advance a novel, unified understanding of latent attention geometry and behavior. We find that sink token functionality is dependent on unintuitive key/query clustering behavior, which RoPE progressively destroys over longer sequences. This is demonstrated empirically and theoretically, establishing two necessary criteria for length generalization: cluster decay must be lower-bounded, and the lower bound must be attained within the training length. Our method RoPE-ID straightforwardly fulfills both criteria, outperforming prior designs, which do not, on long-range retrieval and reasoning benchmarks. RoPE-ID also performs on par with test-time YaRN scaling, but without the need for inference-time model adjustment, and raises scores across the board when combined with YaRN tuning, achieving consistent improvements up to 128k sequence length. This demonstrates the practical utility of our analysis, and unified understanding of attention. 
___

## Reviewer Concerns

Initial scores were **4, 10, 6, and 4**. The majority of concerns were shared between reviewers, with important points falling into four main areas (corresponding to points 1, 2, 3, and 5 in our response to all reviewers):

**1: Lack of clarity in how RoPE-ID achieves length generalization (R1,R4)**. The initial submission did not make the two necessary criteria from our above summary explicitly clear, leading to some confusion in how RoPE-ID functions, and to what rhetorical purpose. In our response we articulate both criteria, and clarify that RoPE-ID is one simple way to fulfill them, while prior methods (other than YaRN) do not. This leads to better-informed design and superior performance for RoPE-ID, and demonstrates the practical utility of our analysis and proposed unified understanding. 

**2. Lack of ablations on chosen hyperparameters (R1,R3,R4)**. In the initial submission, we employed simple heuristics in RoPE-ID’s design: set the shortest wavelength to 32 and the largest to half the training length, apply rotation to half the channels in each head, and employ YaRN-style temperature scaling at inference time. We performed the requested ablations on all these settings (Appendix A8), finding a general pattern of gently rising scores before a sharp drop. Our choices represent safe middle-ground options.

**3. Lack of theoretical justification/analysis (R1,R3)**. The initial submission relied strictly on empirical observations of key/query latent behavior. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of the impact of RoPE on clustering as measured by matrix stable rank (Appendix A11), aligning with our observations (Fig. 16). 

**4. Limited scope and scale of evaluation (R3,R4)**. Benchmark evaluations in the initial submission were limited to 1B- and 3B-parameter models, and to context length 16k and shorter (4x the training length). In our response we clarify that larger models are not feasible due to our conducting pretraining from scratch, and we limit length to 16k because the performance of all tuning-free methods tends to degrade heavily beyond 4x extension. However, we do find that existing long-context tuning techniques, when applied to RoPE-ID models, improve performance on up to 128k sequence length, compared to tuned baselines (Appendix A9). Thus our results do scale beyond context length 16k.

___

## Discussion Status

Remaining concerns - additional clustering metrics (R1,R3), figure formatting (R1,R2), implementation questions (R2,R4), and individual comments - were, we believe, both less important overall, and addressed more simply and directly. Unfortunately, reviewers did not respond before comments were locked, so we do not know to what degree their concerns were allayed overall. However, we hope that our responses directly addressing each overarching concern, as well as the positive average initial score, are sufficient to recommend acceptance. 

We recognize that the identity leakage and discussion rollback represent unprecedented burdens on area chairs, and hope that this comment serves as a useful summary of the discussion and revisions. We are of course happy to answer any remaining questions or provide additional clarification. 

Thank you for your time and attention,

Authors

We thank the reviewers for their time and thoughtful feedback. We are glad to see that reviewers found that the geometric interpretation connecting RoPE, attention, and sink tokens is **original and intuitive** (R1,R2). The explanation of RoPE’s long-context failure due to geometric disruption is **clear** (R2,R3) and provides **strong motivation** for RoPE-ID (R4). The proposed method is **simple and low-cost** (R2,R3), and the **analysis is thorough** (R1,R2,R3) with **comprehensive experiments** (R4).

We also appreciate reviewers' insightful suggestions and constructive criticism, through which we are able to improve the manuscript and expand upon our original findings. Many questions and concerns were shared among reviewers and so we address them jointly below, in rough order of importance. 

*(Note that tables shown here are better viewed in the updated Appendix. New material starts on page 20, marked blue for convenience)*

___
## 1. Exact mechanism by which RoPE-ID achieves length generalization (R1,R4)
We apologize for the lack of clarity, in that we did not make clear how our proposed geometric understanding of attention informs RoPE-ID. The failure mechanism we identified - loss of sink token functionality due to progressive key/query cluster overlap - establishes the following **two necessary criteria for effective length generalization**. First, **the degree of cluster overlap must be lower-bounded**, so that cluster separation is maintained and the sink token can continue to function in the limit. Second, **this lower bound must be attained within the training length**. Otherwise, clusters may drift sufficiently close to produce OOD behavior over time. Fig 7 in the paper best illustrates these dynamics. Applying standard RoPE to half the channels satisfies the first criterion, but not the second (cluster decay is bounded but continues OOD), and so retrieval capabilities are high within the training length, but fall beyond it. High-frequency RoPE satisfies the second, but not the first (all cluster decay happens inside the training length, but decay is total), and so retrieval capabilities are stable over time, but generally poor. RoPE-ID (and YaRN and other NTK-aware methods) fulfill both criteria and so are able to generalize effectively. We will make this relationship clear in the paper, and emphasize that **these two necessary criteria, as well as the geometric understanding behind them, form the primary contribution of our work**. RoPE-ID is one simple example for how to fulfill these criteria in a straightforward and effective manner. 
___
## 2. Ablations on RoPE-ID design choices and hyperparameters (R1,R3,R4)
The choice of frequencies, number of channels, and degree of temperature scaling in RoPE-ID were based on simple heuristics with an eye toward straightforwardness and generality. Reviewers rightfully point out that these settings should be justified experimentally by ablations, and so **we have added these results below, and to Appendix A8**, using RULER and Llama 1B models. Scores are relatively insensitive to degree of temperature scaling, while for channels/frequencies, scores increase as high-frequency RoPE channels are eliminated, especially for short contexts. However, eventually the model reaches a threshold beyond which generalization to longer contexts drops sharply. 
We hypothesize that this is due to the network instead learning to encode position based on learned patterns of latent drift, which do not generalize to longer contexts.
**Thus our chosen values represent a safe middle ground**. For further details, and visually interpretable presentations, please see Appendix A8. We will add this discussion to the main paper.

summary.value:
This paper presents a geometric analysis of Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) to explain long-context failure modes in Transformers. The authors find that RoPE induces tightly clustered query/key point clouds within training length, supporting the formation of sink tokens that prevent over-mixing. However, when input length exceeds training context, RoPE disperses and overlaps these clusters, disabling sink token functionality and causing degraded attention behavior.
Building on this insight, the paper proposes RoPE-ID (In-Distribution), a modification that applies RoPE with high frequency to only a subset of channels, maintaining cluster separation while preserving position information. Experiments on LongBench and RULER with 1B- and 3B-parameter Transformers show that RoPE-ID achieves comparable or superior long-context generalization to tuning-free baselines such as YaRN, without fine-tuning.

strengths.value:
1. The geometric interpretation of RoPE and attention behavior is original, intuitive, and interesting, linking positional encoding, cluster geometry, and sink token dynamics into a unified framework.

2. The paper validates hypotheses through detailed analyses (PCA projections, singular value decomposition, attention maps) and replicates findings across multiple LLM families (LLaMA, Gemma, Olmo).

3. Figures (e.g., cluster diagrams and singular-value ratios) effectively convey geometric intuition and support claims.

4. Addresses a critical bottleneck in scaling LLMs to longer contexts, thus of broad interest to both researchers and practitioners.

weaknesses.value:
1. While the geometric intuition is appealing, the paper lacks a mathematical analysis of how RoPE’s rotation frequencies affect cluster stability. The mechanism by which RoPE transforms i.i.d. token embeddings into clustered structures and subsequently causes cluster dispersion under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions remains insufficiently explained.

2. Figure 2 analyzes cosine similarities, yet attention operates on dot products. This mismatch raises concerns about whether the reported geometric observations truly reflect the behavior of the attention mechanism.

3. The so-called “Unified Theory of RoPE Attention” Section 3.2.2 primarily summarizes prior empirical findings rather than providing a formal theoretical analysis. The term “theory” may therefore be overstated.

4. The proposed RoPE-ID method, which applies RoPE to only half of the channels using higher frequencies, does not convincingly demonstrate that it can effectively mitigate the identified issues. The paper does not clearly explain why this configuration mitigates key/query dispersion, and the presented results suggest the phenomenon is not fully resolved. Moreover, the authors should further analyze the trade-off that higher frequencies blur local positional distinctions.

5. The authors should include ablation studies on the proportion of channels to which RoPE is applied and on the chosen frequency range parameters, to better justify these design choices.

6. Figure 5 lacks proper x-axis labeling, and the notion of “time” used in the caption is ambiguous. Additionally, many figures appear visually unpolished and would benefit from clearer annotations, consistent axis scaling, and improved aesthetics to enhance interpretability.

questions.value: In Figure 7, could the authors clarify the comparison between the configuration with $\theta = 500k$ and the RoPE-ID variant? The plot seems to indicate that the $\theta = 500k$ baseline achieves a higher FSV ratio, implying stronger cluster preservation. Since a smaller $\theta$ corresponds to higher-frequency rotations, why does the high-frequency (orange) curve yield the lowest FSV ratio? This appears to contradict the authors’ claim that higher frequencies should maintain cluster stability.

Thank you for your feedback and constructive criticism! We address weaknesses/questions individually, in order:
___
**W1:** apologies for any confusion, please see shared response 1 for a clearer explanation of the RoPE-ID mechanism. 
While our proposed method is simple and straightforward, we argue it is not trivial, as the design is backed by deep understanding and strong empirical and theoretical support.
In particular, we show that frequency scaling alone does *not* achieve effective length generalization, as cluster separation in the limit requires channels that are entirely RoPE-free. Shared response 1 also clarifies the intended contribution, namely that we provide, for the first time, a unified understanding of the exact failure mechanism for length generalization in transformer models with RoPE. Further, our framework establishes necessary criteria for mitigating this failure mechanism. RoPE-ID serves to illustrate that this knowledge is useful; our goal is not to establish RoPE-ID as a globally superior position encoding scheme, but rather to showcase the benefits of deeper understanding. 

**W2:** we provide ablations on these hyperparameters in shared response 2. 

**W3:** the primary contribution of our work is the elucidation of the length generalization failure mechanism. Again, our goal is not to establish RoPE-ID as a globally superior position encoding scheme. RoPE-ID serves as an illustration of how a simple technique based on the principles established in shared response 1 can perform just as well as YaRN, without requiring test-time adjustment. Even if RoPE-ID is not consistently better (they are accomplishing similar things geometrically, after all), RoPE-ID is simpler, more straightforward, and allows models to generalize by design, rather than requiring input-length-specific scaling of particular parameters at inference time. That said, we do find dramatically improved performance when both methods are combined for tuning at 128k scale (shared response 5).

**W4:** training from scratch is a strong limitation; that said, our goal is to inform the design of *future models* via the proposed geometric understanding, so that they can scale out of the box, by design, without having to rely on inference-time intervention. Whether current RoPE models can be converted to RoPE-ID models, and how this compares to inference-time frequency scaling, is an interesting direction for future work. 
Regarding comparisons to NTK-aware scaling, we do include a baseline based on post-training frequency calibration. Of our four baselines, only RoPE, High Frequency, and HalfRoPE are trained from scratch. The YaRN baseline instead applies test-time frequency scaling to the RoPE model checkpoint. To our knowledge, YaRN builds off of NTK-aware approaches and qualifies as a special case of NTK-by-parts (with temperature scaling). Thus we argue that the strong YaRN baseline does constitute a comparison to NTK-aware scaling.
We will make this clearer in the paper.

**Q1:** thank you for bringing this work to our attention, we will add it to the related work section. To our understanding, the Resonance RoPE methodology is orthogonal to RoPE-ID. 
Resonance RoPE employs integer wavelengths to eliminate phase shifts primarily in high-frequency channels unscaled by YaRN, improving OOD performance. Our method tackles the problem from a geometric perspective and argues that some channels should not apply RoPE at all to avoid OOD issues in the sink token, and that only the high-frequency channels are needed for encoding position. Because Resonance RoPE primarily targets the high-frequency channels, it can be potentially combined with RoPE-ID to further improve performance. We believe that OOD phase shift and sink token functionality are separate problems, and so this combination would likely be quite beneficial.

**Q2:** please see shared response 7. Regarding channel selection: because we are training from scratch, there is no notion of "correctness" tied to the original frequencies, and 
"adaptive" scaling schemes can be implemented via setting the relevant "absolute" hyperparameters to corresponding values. We provide ablations on these hyperparameters in shared response 2.

**Q3:** please see shared response 5. While larger models are not feasible for us due to pretraining costs, we are able to demonstrate improved performance at 128k context length via fine-tuning. 
___
We hope that we have addressed the reviewer's concerns and would be happy to discuss further.

summary.value: This paper analyzes why Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) fails beyond its training context and attributes the issue to geometric degradation in attention. The authors show that key and query vectors form tight clusters and rely on a “sink” token for stability, but RoPE distorts this structure at long ranges. They propose RoPE-ID, which applies high-frequency RoPE to only part of the channels to preserve cluster geometry without fine-tuning. Results on 1B and 3B models show improved long-context performance on LongBench and RULER benchmarks compared to standard RoPE baselines.

Proposes a simple, low-cost remedy (RoPE-ID) that requires no fine-tuning, facilitating rapid deployment.

Demonstrates robust empirical evaluation across tasks and baselines and provides reproducibility details.

[1] Chen, Y., Lv, A., Luan, J., Wang, B., & Liu, W. (2024). *HoPE: A novel positional encoding without long-term decay for enhanced context awareness and extrapolation*. arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.21216.

summary.value: Transformers with RoPE fail on inputs longer than training length. The paper observes that keys and queries form separated clusters, enabling "sink tokens" to absorb default attention. ## 3. Mathematical analysis, especially w.r.t. rotation frequencies (R1,R3)
Thank you for highlighting this weakness; we have produced a new theoretical result characterizing the effect of RoPE, a sketch for which is provided here. The full proof is available in Appendix A11.

The dispersion of clusters can be characterized by the **stable rank**, a continuous analogue of standard matrix rank.
For a matrix $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ with $n>d$, the stable rank of $X$ is defined as $\mathrm{sr}(X):=\frac{\|X\|_F^2}{\|X\|_2^2} =\frac{\sum _{i=1}^d \sigma_i^2}{\sigma_1^2}$, where $\sigma_1\geq \dots \geq \sigma_d$ are the singular values. 
For a key/query matrix $X$, our new theoretical result shows that applying RoPE increases its stable rank (which typically starts close to 1) for large sequence length $n$. This causes its row vectors (i.e., the point cloud) to spread out around the origin as shown in the last panel of Fig. 3.

**Theorem 1** (Informal).
Assume the key/query matrix $X = u v^\top \in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, where $u\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Then, under mild conditions, applying RoPE to $X$ increases its stable rank by at least a factor of 2, and by up to a factor of $d$, provided $n$ is sufficiently large.

The exact scaling factor in $[2,d]$ depends on the underlying learned representation $v$: if $v$ is one-hot, then it rotates through only a single plane, increasing stable rank to 2, while if $v$ is the ones vector, it rotates equally through every plane, increasing stable rank to $d$. Similarly, the rate of scaling also depends on $v$: if $v$ is one-hot in a high frequency channel, the increase will occur quickly, with the opposite for a low-frequency channel, and mixtures landing in between. We will add this discussion to the paper with proof in Appendix A11.
___
## 4. Additional metrics for demonstrating clustering in Fig.2 (R1,R3)
Our thanks for bringing these options to our attention. We have repeated the analysis in Fig.2 and added the results to Appendix A10. **Results are as expected** - dot products yield similar patterns, if more noisily, while stable rank and Davies-Bouldin and Silhouette scores increase/decrease with RoPE and sequence length as expected. ## 7. Why hard-code the first and third quarter of channels? (R2,R4)
Apologies for the confusion! This stems from a quirk in how HuggingFace applies RoPE: the first and third quarters of the *real-valued* channels correspond to the *first half of complex-valued channels*, i.e. the first half of the channel *pairs*. We will update the caption to codeblock 3 to make this clear.

summary.value: The authors propose RoPE-ID, a rotary positional embedding (RoPE) based positional embedding method that scales a proportion of head-specific channels to ensure that long-context inputs are more in-distribution relative to the training data. The authors show that this method is competitive with existing long-context extension techniques on numerous benchmarks on models of multiple sizes.

strengths.value: The authors provide a strong motivation for the method through the analysis of attention sinks and singular values. The experiments are also comprehensive and show some cases of RoPE-ID being beneficial compared to alternative methods.

weaknesses.value:
- The contribution itself remains somewhat trivial; relative to the changes with standard RoPE, it appears that the primary difference is only that low frequency RoPE dimensions are individually scaled such that they can complete the rotation within the provided training length. 

- There is a rather significant lack of clarity regarding the effects of the hyper-parameter choices; for example using half the dimensions in a fixed manner and/or the maximum/minimum frequencies allowed.

- The experimental results are rather unconvincing of the benefits of the method due to some inconsistencies. For example, on RULER, improvements in the 1B model do not appear statistically significant compared to YaRN. Meanwhile, on the 3B model, performance on the 8K context is much better in YaRN but then decreases for 16K. For LongBench, YaRN outperforms RoPE-ID on the 3B model but not the 1B. Thus I cannot gauge exactly what the trend will be for either larger models or more data.

- These models all require training from scratch; this is a rather strong limitation. Additional baselines should include NTK-aware scaling methods, which the authors mention in the related work but do not compare with on downstream tasks. Given the additional complexity of pre-training from scratch, it is further important to compare against methods that calibrate or adjust scaling factors rather than require pre-training new models from scratch as well.

questions.value:
- While the methodology differs, I believe that the underlying phenomena that the authors discuss relates significantly with [1]. In particular, ensuring that the low frequency dimensions complete a rotation is quite related to ensuring that longer relative distances does not appear OOD relative to what was learned during training.

- Based on my understanding of the pseudocode in Appendix A.3, the scaled dimensions are hard-coded as the first quarter and third quarter of the dimensions. Why is this the case and wouldn't it make more sense to apply a more adaptive scaling method that looks at all the dimensions instead and choose a proportion of the dimensions to scale based on the frequency values?

- While I'm not the largest advocate for scaling trends, given the inconsistency in the results the method would be more convincing if either results on larger models or data sizes were provided and showed a more clear trend of the advantages of RoPE-ID relative to existing methods.

[1] Resonance RoPE: Improving Context Length Generalization of Large Language Models
